fields.title: Pirs: Client Sent a Two-Page Spec
fields.summary: A major client described the screen they need down to the last button. Decide what you will design.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you design and release in these six weeks?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Pirs.
fields.brief/company: Pirs is a fictional warehouse receiving system: 40 clients, ranging from a single warehouse to a chain of twelve.
fields.brief/context: The largest client is the Obodok chain (22% of Pirs's revenue). They sent a specification for 'partial receiving': screen, fields, buttons, and workflow. They want it released in six weeks, otherwise they will look for another system.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what you will design and release.
fields.brief/constraints: Six weeks, three developers, half-time designer.
fields.brief/task: Choose an approach and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: The client sends a solution — the problem is still yours
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A ready-made spec saves a conversation but hides the problem: the screen is described, but not why it is needed. Uncovering the actual problem is almost always cheaper than building someone else's sketch, and it usually turns out to be common to many clients. When designing, start with objects and states: if the system cannot represent a discrepancy, no mockup can fix it.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Two pages: a 'Partial Receiving' screen, seven fields, a 'Receive Partially' button, a 'Record Shortage' button, and a print form.

Workflow in the spec: the warehouse worker opens the shipment → checks off the received items → clicks 'Receive Partially' → prints the report.

The reason in the email is stated in a single line: 'We need partial receiving, just like in our previous system.'

Contract value is 22% of Pirs's revenue. It is up for renewal in four months.

In the same email, a separate line: 'And make sure it works in one click.'
fields.evidenceCards/1/title: A day at the Obodok warehouse
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
You visited the warehouse and shadowed a shift.

A truck arrives, and the warehouse worker checks the items against the invoice. Discrepancies come in three types: shortage, wrong item, or damaged goods. During the shift, this happened four times out of seventeen deliveries.

Currently, for any discrepancy, the worker calls the shift supervisor, who calls the supplier. The delivery hangs for 20–40 minutes, and the truck just sits there.

In Pirs, the worker can do nothing at this point: the system accepts the delivery either in full or not at all. So they accept it in full and text the supervisor about the discrepancy on WhatsApp.

At the end of the shift, the supervisor manually compiles these messages into a spreadsheet for accounting. Twice last month, they got lost.

Workers say 'shortage', 'wrong item', 'damaged'. Nobody used the term 'partial receiving'.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Objects: shipment, shipment item, product, warehouse, employee.

Shipment states: expected → receiving → received. There is no separate state for a discrepancy.

A shipment item has an expected quantity but no actual quantity: the system assumes they are equal.

There is no 'discrepancy' object at all — meaning there is nothing to show to accounting, nothing to send to the supplier, and no data to generate a report from.

Print forms are generated from the shipment; therefore, there is currently no way to generate a discrepancy report.

Development estimates: adding actual quantity to the item plus the 'discrepancy' object will take two weeks, and the screens will take another two.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What is happening with other clients
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Support tickets over the last six months, 40 clients:

'How to log a shortage' — 61 tickets from 23 clients.
'How to cancel a received shipment' — 44 tickets from 19 clients (workaround: receive in full, then roll back).
'Need a discrepancy report' — 28 tickets from 14 clients.
'Partial receiving' as a term — 2 tickets, both from Obodok.

Two clients left in the last six months; in the exit survey, one cited 'receiving does not reflect warehouse reality' as the reason.

All three competing systems on the market have this feature.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Uncover the actual problem and design starting from objects
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Find out what the warehouse worker is trying to do when a discrepancy occurs, introduce the missing objects and states, design the flow with all branches, and name the screen using warehouse terminology.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
A conversation with the shift supervisor clarifies the task: not to 'receive partially', but to 'record a discrepancy so the truck can leave, and accounting and the supplier are notified automatically.'
This means you need a 'discrepancy' object and an actual quantity field on the item — taking two weeks — and only then the screens.
The screen is named 'Receiving with Discrepancy', and the types are 'shortage', 'wrong item', and 'damaged', just like they say at the warehouse. Training the workers takes minutes.
New branches appear in the flow that weren't in the spec: discrepancies for damaged goods (the spec only had quantity) and canceling an already completed receiving process.
It is released in the fifth week. Obodok accepts it, even though the screen doesn't match their sketch: the argument took only one meeting because you showed them a shift at their own warehouse.
Within a month, 26 out of 40 clients use the feature, and 'how to log a shortage' tickets drop to three.
Trade-off: the first two weeks looked like 'nothing is happening' from the outside, which had to be explained.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The client represents 22% of revenue and their contract is up in four months. Everything is detailed in the spec, and arguing is costly. Do exactly what is described.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
After two weeks, it turns out there is nowhere to save the item checkboxes: there is no actual quantity field on the item. You have to build the same backend objects anyway, but in a rush and without proper planning.
The screen is released in the sixth week, exactly matching the sketch. Obodok is happy for exactly one week.
Then come questions that weren't in the spec: how to log damaged goods, how to cancel an accidental receiving, where accounting gets the report. Each requires a new patch.
The other 39 clients barely find the feature: it is called 'partial receiving', while they are looking for 'shortage'.
Trade-off: you built a solution tailored to one client's vocabulary and ended up needing the same objects anyway, just at a higher cost and later.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The designer draws screens based on the spec, you show them to Obodok, collect feedback, and then hand them over to development. This way, the client sees progress.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Mockups are ready in a week, the client is happy, and relations are smooth.
During planning, development asks where the actual quantity is stored and what data is used to generate the report. There is no answer: these objects do not exist.
Two weeks are spent rebuilding the model, and some mockups have to be redesigned.
The feature is released in the seventh week — late, despite your promises to the client.
Trade-off: the workflow was reversed, and the approved mockups became a promise you had no way to deliver on.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Build an impact map and prioritize
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Link the request to Pirs's goals — client retention and reducing support tickets — see what behavior needs to change, and prioritize based on that.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The map is built in half a day and yields the correct conclusion: the problem is common, 23 out of 40 clients ask about shortages, this is about retention, not just a concession to Obodok. The prioritization discussion with management is settled immediately.
But the map doesn't answer what exactly to design. The team starts working on screens with the same spec in hand and hits the wall of missing objects in the third week.
The release slips to the seventh week.
Trade-off: the priority was justified correctly, but the solution was designed in the wrong order.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The feature is described in isolation, without the pain point and the benefit on the other side
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The chain from goal to behavior is incomplete, making it unclear why this needs to be done
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Objects and their states are not defined before designing screens
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The flow is designed only for the happy path: empty, error, and conflict states are ignored
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Consistency and interface language are treated as cosmetic issues
